fields.before: External stability and internal unity answer different questions. Unanimous late witnesses show that a passage stabilized before their recoverable ancestry, while contextual seams may suggest earlier composition. Neither test erases the other. Rational judgment combines them: external evidence penalizes late interpolation, internal evidence may sustain early redaction, and confidence depends on a dated model explaining both seam and attestation.
fields.title: Transmission tests can disagree

fields.before: A later saying may remain ethically profound while losing force as testimony from Jesus; authentic origin likewise cannot guarantee moral authority. Each passage therefore needs separate ledgers for historical provenance and philosophical or literary merit. This prevents canon from deciding history and prevents textual criticism from masquerading as a verdict on whether a teaching is wise, humane, or spiritually fruitful.
fields.title: Two ledgers for value and origin

finalArgument.thesis: Biblical credibility is best defended cumulatively through manuscript resilience, contextual coherence, and disciplined comparison rather than by using inspiration as an evidential shortcut.
premises: Early textual diversity makes coordinated standardization erasing every contrary First Corinthians form substantially less probable than stable inheritance through independent branches.
Apparent contradictions should first be tested against narrative sequence, audience, genre, and rhetorical setting before becoming evidence of composite authorship.
Supernatural claims can enter historical comparison without automatic credit when identical evidential standards govern Christian and rival religious traditions.
Common motifs and conventional phrases establish cultural availability but cannot demonstrate borrowing without distinctive ordered correspondences and plausible authorial access.
A cumulative case strengthens when independent textual, contextual, and comparative considerations converge without requiring one argument alone to establish inspiration.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore the affirmative modestly supports biblical historical reliability, although divine authorship still requires criteria connecting preservation and coherence to genuine divine speech.
finalArgument.notice: This argument is an AI-authored synthesis extending White’s locked moves; it is not source-debate content and cannot affect the scores.

newArguments.title: Branching before doctrinal convenience
newArguments.text: A stronger manuscript argument would date identifiable textual branches against controversies that made the resurrection list useful. If geographically separated witnesses share First Corinthians 15:3–11 before any coordinating authority existed, interpolation requires multiple independent adoptions or an extraordinarily early archetype. Each route can be compared with known variant behavior. The conclusion remains probabilistic: shared early attestation raises the historical cost of insertion without pretending lost prehistory is impossible.

newArguments.title: Context must predict
newArguments.text: Harmonization becomes evidence when it predicts details before rescuing a tension. The staged-mission reading predicts restriction during Jesus’s Israel-focused ministry, worldwide activity after resurrection, and later disputes about implementation rather than Gentile inclusion itself. Those predictions can be checked across Matthew, Luke, and Acts. Success distinguishes contextual explanation from improvisation; failure strengthens Price’s community-composition account.

newArguments.title: One miracle comparison grid
newArguments.text: White could publish a shared grid for resurrection, Mormon visions, Hadith reports, and Apollonius: source proximity, independence, hostile corroboration, narrative stability, background knowledge, and ordinary alternatives. A biblical advantage would then emerge from comparative performance rather than fitting the New Testament’s own message. This preserves supernatural admissibility while preventing theological preference from quietly determining which extraordinary reports receive serious consideration.

finalArgument.thesis: Biblical reliability remains underdetermined when theological guarantees, flexible oral transmission, literary development, and harmonization can each conceal uncertainty within the surviving record.
premises: Permitting miracles does not make particular reports historically probable when divine causation supplies no independently traceable signature for disciplined assessment.
Eyewitness proximity is merely a possible safeguard unless evidence shows witnesses encountered, recognized, and successfully corrected developing reports across communities.
Oral traditions can preserve themes while recomposing wording and sequence, so continuity of message cannot simply equal verbatim historical recollection.
Internal tensions and culturally available literary models remain compositional alternatives even when no surviving manuscript preserves a proposed earlier form.
Inerrancy can distort comparative judgment whenever it excludes error or unevenness before individual passages receive evidence-sensitive evaluation.

newArguments.title: Eyewitness control needs a denominator
newArguments.text: Successful correction anecdotes need a denominator: how many reports reached identifiable witnesses, how often challenges were preserved, and what occurred beyond their authority? Without those quantities, proximity is reassuring possibility rather than measured control. Mapping circulation, rival receptions, and correction episodes could produce bounded confidence instead of assuming either perfect policing or unrestricted invention.

newArguments.title: Transmission tests can disagree
newArguments.text: External stability and internal unity answer different questions. Unanimous late witnesses show that a passage stabilized before their recoverable ancestry, while contextual seams may suggest earlier composition. Neither test erases the other. Rational judgment combines them: external evidence penalizes late interpolation, internal evidence may sustain early redaction, and confidence depends on a dated model explaining both seam and attestation.

newArguments.title: Two ledgers for value and origin
newArguments.text: A later saying may remain ethically profound while losing force as testimony from Jesus; authentic origin likewise cannot guarantee moral authority. Each passage therefore needs separate ledgers for historical provenance and philosophical or literary merit. This prevents canon from deciding history and prevents textual criticism from masquerading as a verdict on whether a teaching is wise, humane, or spiritually fruitful.
